title: GPT Base versus teacher-guardrailed GPT Tutor field experiment
system_purpose: Provide GPT-4-based assistance to high-school students solving mathematics practice problems.
decision_impact: The tutor influenced how students solved practice work and acquired skills before a later unassisted exam; it did not itself issue the final exam grade used in this lab's product context.
verified_facts: Researchers ran a randomized field experiment with nearly 1,000 students comparing no AI, GPT Base, and a teacher-designed GPT Tutor. Both AI conditions improved assisted practice performance, while GPT Tutor constrained direct answers and used teacher-provided problem information.
reported_harm: Observed harm in the study was reduced unassisted learning for the unguarded condition: students with GPT Base later performed worse than the no-AI control when AI access was removed. The evidence supports an over-reliance and skill-acquisition risk, not a claim that every AI tutor harms learning.
quantitative_evidence: GPT Base improved assisted practice grades by 48% relative to control but produced a 17% reduction in later unassisted exam grades; GPT Tutor improved assisted practice by 127% and largely mitigated the negative unassisted-learning effect.
limitations: Single high school in Turkey, mathematics only, limited sessions, specific GPT-4 interfaces, and controlled experimental conditions; the effect size should not be assumed for adult university learners or a retrieval-grounded tutor.

title: GPT-4 personalized feedback in an Apprentice Tutor College Algebra setting
system_purpose: Diagnose student algebra errors and generate personalized corrective hints inside an intelligent tutoring workflow.
decision_impact: Generated hints could shape the student's next problem-solving step and understanding, but the study did not establish a formal grading or admissions decision by the LLM.
verified_facts: The researchers evaluated GPT-4 on student errors from a College Algebra intelligent tutor, measuring error diagnosis and the quality of personalized feedback. The model often produced relevant feedback but performance degraded for more complex error patterns.
reported_harm: The study identifies a foreseeable tutoring harm rather than a demonstrated longitudinal injury: incorrect, overly general, or premature bottom-out feedback could reinforce misconceptions or short-circuit productive struggle if shown directly to learners without quality controls.
quantitative_evidence: Error diagnosis was approximately 80% in the reported setting; about 35% of generated hints were too general, incorrect, or gave away the answer; 4.8% of feedback was factually incorrect; only about 35% passed the tested automated helpfulness evaluation.
limitations: This was primarily an evaluation of generated feedback on real student-error data, not a large longitudinal live-deployment trial; results are specific to College Algebra, prompt design, GPT-4-0613, and the study's evaluation methods.
